s:
Match List-I with List-II regarding centres of the Indus bead industry:

List-I (Centre)
a. Chanhudaro
b. Lothal
c. Kalibangan
 d. Rakhigarhi

List-II (Evidence)
i. Gemstone factory with over 3,000 semi-precious stones
ii. Bead-making factory
iii. Bead-making centre
iv. Bead workshops and carnelian beads for export

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
x: Chanhudaro had a bead-making factory, Lothal had bead workshops and exported carnelian beads, Kalibangan was a bead-making centre, and Rakhigarhi had a gemstone factory with over 3,000 semi-precious stones.
tq: Start from the sure centre–evidence pairs and eliminate codes containing a wrong pair.

s: Which one of the following combinations of materials was used in Indus bead-making?
o: Carnelian, agate, jasper, steatite, lapis lazuli, faience and gold
Iron, mica, asbestos, ivory, lead and tin
Coal, platinum, nickel, limestone, gypsum and amber
Granite, marble, zinc, mercury, iron and glass
x: Indus bead-makers used carnelian, agate, jasper, steatite, lapis lazuli, faience and gold.
tq: Test a complete material list against closely related but unsupported mineral groups.

s:
Consider the following statements regarding Indus bead trade:
1. Carnelian was obtained from Saurashtra.
2. Carnelian beads were exported to Mesopotamia and the Persian Gulf.
3. Lothal was associated with carnelian bead workshops.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Carnelian came from Saurashtra, carnelian beads were exported to Mesopotamia and the Persian Gulf, and Lothal had bead workshops associated with this trade.
tq: Use the option containing all three supported trade links after checking each statement independently.

s: The gemstone factory containing over 3,000 semi-precious stones has been associated with which Indus site?
x: Rakhigarhi has been associated with a gemstone factory containing over 3,000 semi-precious stones.
tq: Use the distinctive numerical clue to identify the corresponding archaeological site.

s:
Match the following sculptures with their sites and materials:

List-I (Sculpture)
a. Dancing Girl
b. Priest-King
c. Nude male torso
d. Dancer torso

List-II (Site and material)
i. Harappa – sandstone
ii. Mohenjodaro – bronze
iii. Harappa – red sandstone
iv. Mohenjodaro – steatite

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
x: The Dancing Girl is from Mohenjodaro and is bronze; the Priest-King is from Mohenjodaro and is steatite; the nude male torso is Harappan red sandstone; and the dancer torso is Harappan sandstone.
tq: Anchor the matching exercise with the two Mohenjodaro sculptures before resolving the Harappa pairs.
sec: Sculpture → site + material (Dancing Girl, Priest-King, Harappa torsos)

s:
The Dancing Girl of the Indus Valley Civilization is associated with which of the following descriptions?
1. It was excavated in 1926 by Ernest Mackay under John Marshall.
2. It is shown in a tribhanga posture.
3. Its right hand is placed on the hip and its left arm is covered with bangles.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: All three statements describe the Dancing Girl: its excavation in 1926, its tribhanga posture, and its characteristic hand and bangle details.
tq: Check the excavation detail and the two visual attributes separately before selecting the complete combination.
sec: Sculpture → site + material (Dancing Girl, Priest-King, Harappa torsos)

s: The Dancing Girl sculpture is generally dated to approximately:
x: The Dancing Girl is dated to approximately 2500 BCE.
tq: Distinguish the closely spaced chronological alternatives by recalling the sculpture’s approximate date.
sec: Sculpture → site + material (Dancing Girl, Priest-King, Harappa torsos)

s: Which one of the following features is associated with the Priest-King sculpture of Mohenjodaro?
o: A tribhanga posture with bangles covering both arms
A seated driver holding the reins of a toy cart
A clean-shaven face and a crown with animal horns
A beard, a forehead fillet and a shawl over one shoulder
x: The Priest-King is represented as bearded, with a fillet on the forehead and a shawl over one shoulder.
tq: Use the person–feature trap by separating the Priest-King’s attributes from those of the Dancing Girl and terracotta figures.
sec: Sculpture → site + material (Dancing Girl, Priest-King, Harappa torsos)

s: The shawl of the Priest-King sculpture bears which design?
x: The shawl of the Priest-King bears a trefoil pattern.
tq: Test the exact iconographic detail rather than the broader description of the sculpture.
sec: Sculpture → site + material (Dancing Girl, Priest-King, Harappa torsos)

s: Which of the following statements about Indus pottery is correct?
o: It was predominantly blue pottery with white script inscriptions.
It was exclusively handmade and normally left unpainted.
It was made only from faience and glazed glass.
It was generally wheel-made, with red pottery carrying black painted designs.
x: Indus pottery was wheel-made; red pottery with black painted designs was typical, alongside plain red and painted red-and-black varieties.
tq: Identify the precise production method and colour combination while rejecting absolute alternatives.
sec: Pottery - colour, design motifs, perforated jars

s: The designs painted on typical Indus pottery were mainly:
x: The principal motifs on Indus pottery were geometric and floral.
tq: Use the exact motif pair and reject distractors that introduce unsupported themes.
sec: Pottery - colour, design motifs, perforated jars

s: Glazed pottery, described as the world’s first, was associated with which material combination?
x: The glazed pottery described as the world’s first was associated with faience and mosaic glass.
tq: Discriminate between pottery materials and the metals or stones used in other crafts.
sec: Pottery - colour, design motifs, perforated jars

s: Perforated jars of the Indus Civilization were characterised by:
o: A large hole at the base and small holes over the wall
A pointed base and a single hole in the lid
A small opening at the base and a large hole on the wall
A completely sealed body with no opening
x: Perforated jars had a large hole at the base and several small holes over the wall, probably for straining liquor.
tq: Pay attention to the reversed size and location of the holes, a common comparison trap.
sec: Pottery - colour, design motifs, perforated jars

s: Which one of the following pairs is NOT correctly matched?
o: Harappa — reserved slip ware of Mesopotamian type
Chanhudaro — reserved slip ware of Mesopotamian type
x: Reserved slip ware of Mesopotamian type is associated with Harappa, not Chanhudaro. Kalibangan had six types of pottery and Lothal had painted jars.
tq: Find the site–pottery pair that does not belong to the stated distribution.
sec: Pottery - colour, design motifs, perforated jars

s:
In the lost-wax or cire perdue technique, the correct sequence is:
A. The wax model is coated with clay.
B. The mould is heated and the wax melts out.
C. Molten metal is poured into the hollow mould.
D. The clay mould is removed after cooling.

Select the correct chronological order.
x: In the lost-wax process, a wax model is coated with clay, heated to remove the wax, filled with molten metal, and finally freed by removing the clay mould.
tq: Arrange the process by identifying the preparation, melting, casting and removal stages.

s: Which of the following groups consists entirely of objects associated with the lost-wax technique?
o: Painted jar, perforated jar, faience bead
Steatite seal, silver vessel, terracotta whistle
Dancing Girl, copper dog and bird of Lothal, bronze bull of Kalibangan
x: The Dancing Girl, the copper dog and bird of Lothal, and the bronze bull of Kalibangan are associated with the lost-wax technique.
tq: Group the objects linked to one production technique and eliminate items made of unrelated materials.

s:
Which of the following statements regarding metal casting in the post-urban phase is correct?
1. Metal casting continued into the Late Harappan and Chalcolithic cultures.
2. The Daimabad bronzes provide an example of this continuity.
3. Metal casting ended completely with the decline of the Mature Harappan cities.

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
x: Metal casting continued into the Late Harappan and Chalcolithic cultures, as illustrated by the Daimabad bronzes. Therefore, the statement that it ended completely is false.
tq: Reject the absolute statement and retain the two statements showing cultural continuity.

s: Which category constituted the most important clay figures of the Indus Civilization?
x: Mother Goddess figurines were the most important clay figures of the Indus Civilization.
tq: Identify the principal category rather than a secondary group of terracotta objects.
sec: Terracotta figurines - mother goddess, animals, toy carts

s: Which of the following is NOT associated with Indus terracotta figurines and toys?
o: Toy carts with seated drivers at Chanhudaro
Whistles, rattles, birds, gamesmen and discs
x: Iron horse-drawn chariots are not listed among the Indus terracotta figurines and toys. The great humpless bull, Chanhudaro toy carts, whistles, rattles, birds, gamesmen and discs are associated with them.
tq: Use the material trap to distinguish documented terracotta objects from an unsupported iron object.
sec: Terracotta figurines - mother goddess, animals, toy carts

s: Lifelike bearded males with coiled hair and a clay mask of a horned god have been associated with:
x: These terracotta representations have been associated with Gujarat and Kalibangan.
tq: Match the distinctive figurine description with its geographical association.
sec: Terracotta figurines - mother goddess, animals, toy carts

s:
Match the following metal objects with their sites and metals:

List-I (Object)
a. Dog chasing a deer
b. Dog and bird
c. Bull or ox
d. Chariot, bull, buffalo, rhinoceros and elephant

List-II (Site and metal)
i. Lothal – copper
ii. Harappa – bronze
iii. Kalibangan – bronze or copper
iv. Daimabad – bronze or copper

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
x: The dog chasing a deer is a bronze object from Harappa; the dog and bird are copper objects from Lothal; the bull or ox is from Kalibangan; and the larger animal group is from Daimabad.
tq: Begin with the distinctive Harappa and Lothal pairs, then separate Kalibangan from Daimabad.
sec: Metal crafts - copper, bronze, gold, silver objects

s: Which of the following groups contains only tools mentioned among Indus metal crafts?
o: Hammers, drills, chains, wheels and lamps
Chisels, needles, fishhooks, razors, mirrors, axes and celts
Ploughs, sickles, locks, coins and anchors
Swords, cannons, guns, helmets and shields
x: The listed Indus metal tools included chisels, needles, fishhooks, razors, mirrors, axes and celts.
tq: Select the exact documented tool group instead of a broader modern equipment list.
sec: Metal crafts - copper, bronze, gold, silver objects

s:
Which statement correctly describes the vessels and ornaments associated with Indus metal crafts?
1. Vessels were made of copper, bronze and silver.
2. Gold and silver necklaces were found at Allahdino.
3. Rakhigarhi had a gold foundry with an active furnace.

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
x: Copper, bronze and silver vessels, gold and silver necklaces at Allahdino, and a gold foundry with an active furnace at Rakhigarhi are all documented features.
tq: Check the three separate evidence points before choosing the complete combination.
sec: Metal crafts - copper, bronze, gold, silver objects

s: Which animal motif was the most common on steatite seals of the Indus Civilization?
x: The unicorn was the most common animal motif on Indus steatite seals; bull, elephant, tiger and rhinoceros were also represented.
tq: Distinguish the most frequent motif from other genuine but less common seal animals.

s:
Consider the following statements about Indus seals:
1. They were commonly carved from steatite.
2. Their motifs included animals and the Pashupati figure.
3. Short lines of script were also present on them.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
x: Indus seals were commonly made of steatite, displayed animal and Pashupati motifs, and carried short script lines.
tq: Combine material, iconography and inscription evidence without confusing seals with pottery decoration.

s: Which pair of techniques was listed together as new techniques of the Indus period?
x: Carving seals and working carnelian were listed together as new techniques of the period.
tq: Identify the exact paired technological development rather than selecting later innovations.

s:
Which of the following sites is associated with shell-working evidence?
1. Nageshwar
2. Balakot
3. Lothal
4. Chanhudaro

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
x: Shell-working evidence is associated with Nageshwar, Balakot and Lothal, while Chanhudaro had a shell-ornament factory.
tq: Count all the sites linked to shell work, including the specialised factory at Chanhudaro.

s: Shell bangles found in burials have been reported from which site?
x: Shell bangles have been reported from Rakhigarhi burials.
tq: Use the burial context to distinguish Rakhigarhi from other shell-working locations.

s: Which of the following products were made of faience in the Indus Civilization?
x: Faience was used for beads, bangles and glazed ware, and its association with mosaic glass provides an early clue to glass-making.
tq: Separate faience products from metal tools, stone sculpture and precious-metal ornaments.

s: The faience–mosaic glass association provides an early clue to the development of:
x: The association of faience with mosaic glass provides an early clue to glass-making.
tq: Infer the technological implication directly from the material association.

s: The original image of the Dancing Girl is proposed to be restored in which educational context?
o: A museum catalogue of Harappan seals
A new Class 9 Art textbook of NCERT
A university handbook on ancient metallurgy
A Class 6 archaeology textbook of the Archaeological Survey of India
x: NCERT is to restore the original image of the Dancing Girl in its new Class 9 Art textbook.
tq: Identify the institution and educational level in the current-relevance statement.

s: The naturalistic bronze and stone sculptures of the Indus Civilization primarily indicate:
o: The complete absence of specialised artisans
The use of sculpture only for royal portraits
x: The naturalistic quality of bronze and stone sculpture indicates advanced metallurgical skill and craft specialisation.
tq: Connect the artistic evidence with the broader economic and technological inference.

s:
Which of the following statements is correct regarding two distinctive features of the Indus Civilization?
1. Glazed pottery has been described as the world’s first.
2. Chanhudaro is the only Indus city without a citadel.
3. Lothal is the only Indus city without a citadel.

Select the correct answer using the codes given below.
x: Glazed pottery has been described as the world’s first, and Chanhudaro is the only Indus city without a citadel. The statement about Lothal is incorrect.
tq: Use the unique-status trap by distinguishing Chanhudaro from another important Indus site.
